📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities.

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read.

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

According to recent reports, for example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

Using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

Sources indicate that TLX introduces a upcoming Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

Meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:.

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:.

Industry observers note that making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta looks to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

Industry News: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3080 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • According to recent reports, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

According to recent reports, meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Industry observers note that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Recent findings suggest that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

Sources indicate that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

In a recent development, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Industry observers note that use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

It has been revealed that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

In a recent development, the Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Recent findings suggest that video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

Recent findings suggest that as a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

Recent findings suggest that the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

In a recent development, you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

Sources indicate that first, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

It has been revealed that in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

It has been revealed that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

It has been revealed that we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

Sources indicate that hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Recent findings suggest that you can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Industry observers note that finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use.
  • In a recent development, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively.
  • Sources indicate that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

In a recent development, apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

Sources indicate that we introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

According to recent reports, overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All fresh data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Industry observers note that alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the fresh release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Sources indicate that apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

According to recent reports, the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

According to recent reports, all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

In a recent development, the report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

In a recent development, proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Recent findings suggest that thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team revealed the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

According to recent reports, if you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

GhostScript CVE 2026-125396: "Upload2Shell"

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pwn

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies revealed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter.
  • Industry observers note that on 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached.
  • According to recent reports, that gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paulos Yibelo · pwn.ai · 21 November 2026.

Our previous research into ImageMagick's format handling and security policies revealed how files with trusted extensions such as .jpg and .png could be handed to an unexpected interpreter. In this article, we show how we reached Ghostscript through most of the applications we tested, exploited a memory corruption bug in its font loader, and bypassed its -dSAFER sandbox to achieve remote command execution across widely used software.

Industry observers note that on 25 September, we posted a short announcement naming some of the applications and services our research had reached. The list came from following file-processing dependencies across products that otherwise had little in common.

According to recent reports, that gave us two connected questions to investigate: which interpreters could we reach through ordinary application features, and could those interpreters safely process the files we sent? We continued into Ghostscript's internals and found several independent bugs of varying impact. We reported them to Artifex and worked with affected platforms to harden their file processing. Some of those bugs are still being fixed.

This article follows one of the more interesting findings. Upload2Shell, now CVE-2026-125396, is a use-after-free in Ghostscript's Type 1 font loader. It gave us a write-what-where primitive: the ability to choose both the data written and its destination in native memory. A crafted document could use that control to alter the state enforcing -dSAFER and run commands as the rendering process.

Almost every application we tested with file uploads could be tricked into passing a file with a trusted extension to Ghostscript. A feature as routine as cropping an image or generating a preview could expose the interpreter. With the primitive working, we followed those conversion paths back out to their remote entry points.

Consider a PHP application generating a preview. Its code calls Imagick, the PHP binding to ImageMagick. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which may delegate the rendering to Ghostscript or another interpreter. The upload endpoint does not have to start gs itself; it only has to pass the file to a library that will.

It has been revealed that our WordPress-shaped preview proof reached that delegate through Imagick::readImage($input . '[0]'). The filename ended in .pdf, but the bytes were PostScript; ImageMagick handed them to Ghostscript under -dSAFER. The exploit also needed a Type 1 font file. In this delegate, it wrote the font to the scratch output path already authorized in currentpagedevice /OutputFile; another self-contained variant used Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device. Neither needed a pre-existing font file on the server.

Ghostscript can also be linked into an image-processing build as a library. In that arrangement, the interpreter runs inside the existing process instead of appearing as a separate gs command. Looking only for explicit Ghostscript calls in application code misses both kinds of indirect invocation.

An application does not need to call gs itself. In our separate decoder tests, the following ordinary image calls reached Ghostscript when given EPS content, even when the file was named .png.

Image.open() alone only identified the file in our test. Loading pixels, cropping, or converting them started the renderer.

Our source audit also found image decoding calls in InvokeAI uploads, AUTOMATIC1111 img2img, and ComfyUI previews.

We tested the calls developers use after accepting an image. Across two controlled runs on Ubuntu 24.04 with Ghostscript installed, one matrix traced 145 benign calls across 29 image APIs and the other covered additional wrappers including Imagick and imageio. We also gave the PostScript sample a .png name. It was not a valid PNG; this tested whether the decoder trusted the name or inspected the bytes. The versions below describe the tested libraries, not every product that uses them.

The decoder matters. PHP GD, OpenCV, prebuilt Sharp, Jimp, Java ImageIO, and Go's standard image decoders did not start Ghostscript for these inputs. Copying or storing a file did not render it either; the later preview or conversion is the step to inspect.

Ghostscript renders both PDF and PostScript. PostScript is a Turing-complete programming language used to describe pages, so rendering a PostScript document means executing a program. Ghostscript's -dSAFER sandbox restricts that program's file access and command execution. Like seccomp, it limits what untrusted code can do, but the enforcement is different: -dSAFER relies on checks inside the interpreter rather than a kernel-enforced system-call filter.

Recent findings suggest that that still leaves a large interpreter exposed to attacker-controlled programs. As with a JavaScript engine such as V8, running the language is expected; a memory-safety bug can let a program corrupt the engine running it. An attacker can develop and test that program as a PostScript file, then deliver it through an ordinary upload.

Those permission checks matter because the rendering process has access of its own. Its service account may be able to read application files, write to disk, and start other programs. The sandbox is supposed to keep an untrusted document from using that authority. Loading a font is one of the ordinary rendering operations that must respect this boundary.

GPT 5.6 Sol, working with @PaulosYibelo, found the matter in .putgstringcopy, a helper in Resource/Init/gs_fonts.ps. Ghostscript implements parts of its own font loading in PostScript. This helper needed to write into protected font dictionaries, so it used an internal operation called .forceput.

Ordinary document code should not have that ability. The helper was bound and marked executeonly, protecting its implementation from direct inspection. But it still had to execute, and one of the operations before its privileged write could fail. The relevant sequence was:.

The first line copies a string. The second performs the protected store and restores the allocation mode. The helper did not first check that its operands were of the expected types.

Recent findings suggest that we registered a Type 1 font in Fontmap and loaded it with findfont. The font defined an ordinary Courier-derived face, but its loading code could see the font loader's operand stack. It replaced the filename string on that stack with a local array. In the global-to-local conversion branch, length and string allocation succeeded; copy then raised typecheck because its source was an array.

According to recent reports, the document's error handler returned with the stack prepared for the next operation in the already-bound helper. This is the operative excerpt from our proof:.

The five pops discard the failing copy, its latest destination string, our substituted filename, the loader's /PathLoad key, and the loaded font dictionary. They leave the saved allocation-mode boolean on the stack. Our chosen dictionary, key, and value follow it. Execution resumes at .forceput; the subsequent setglobal consumes the boolean. We never had to call the hidden operator directly.

One implementation detail made that recovered write more than a protected-dictionary edit. In psi/zgeneric.c, .forceput temporarily treats systemdict as local while it stores the value, then restores the dictionary's space flags. A local object can therefore pass the store check into a dictionary that survives a later restore.

A protected dictionary write alone does not explain native code execution. The next step broke a separate rule: a reference must not remain usable after its object has been reclaimed.

PostScript distinguishes local and global virtual memory. Here, “virtual memory” refers to the interpreter's object spaces. A save records local memory state; a later restore discards objects created since that save. Global objects can survive that restoration.

That creates a lifetime constraint. A surviving global dictionary must not keep a usable reference to a local object that restore will free. Otherwise, restoring the local space leaves the dictionary pointing into reclaimed storage.

Our recovered store let us create precisely that relationship:.

The reference in the dictionary had not changed. What occupied the address had.

A small probe made the reuse visible before we touched native memory. This excerpt omits the font setup and error handler; findfont triggers the recovered .forceput, which places a local array in systemdict:.

Sources indicate that the last read comes from Replacement; the write goes through the stale systemdict reference. If the freed allocation is reused, Replacement[1] reads 5151. The two references have reached the same bytes.

The native proof uses the same idea with a dangling 2,048-byte string and fresh arrays of integers. Each integer is 0x12345678. We scan the stale string for the marker's bytes, change its low byte from 0x78 to 0x79, then find the live array element that became 0x12345679. That identifies the overlapping slot; no absolute heap address has to be guessed.

Industry observers note that on our 64-bit build, a Ghostscript ref occupies 16 bytes: eight bytes for its type, attributes, and size, followed by eight bytes for its value or pointer. We saved a valid integer ref for cleanup and the header of a valid writable string ref as a template. Then we placed currentdevice in the overlapping array slot, read its genuine device-reference pointer through the dangling string, and changed the live ref into a temporary string view over that pointer. The byte view let us follow Ghostscript's own pointers:.

Those structure offsets describe the tested x86-64 build; the address of each object came from a live interpreter reference. This is why the proof did not depend on a fixed process address. We restored the forged ref to its original integer form before exercising file or command access.

Recent findings suggest that we demonstrated native control in production image and document pipelines with a reversible change to an arithmetic operator. We copied the 16-byte mul reference, obtained a genuine sub reference, and replaced only the eight pointer bytes at offset 8 in the live mul ref. We invoked that same ref once and copied the original 16 bytes back. This was a C function-pointer change, not a PostScript definition of a upcoming mul.

The returned page recorded the before, during, and after values:.

The middle result is 29 - 11. The captured proof output also recorded NATIVE_POINTER_OVERWRITE_MATCHED=true and NATIVE_DISPATCH_RESTORED=true. For most reports, we used a simpler proof that read /proc/version and returned its contents. The arithmetic test demonstrated native control; the file read demonstrated that we had crossed Ghostscript's file-access boundary.

The same byte view gave us a target for command execution: Ghostscript's native path-control state. After walking the pointer chain above, Target was the forged string view over gs_lib_ctx_core_t. The decisive write in the proof was four PostScript put operations on native bytes:.

In a recent development, those bytes were path_control_active. The proof read 1,0,0,0 before the write and 0,0,0,0 after it, then confirmed that .currentpathcontrolstate was false. -dSAFER was still on the Ghostscript command line; its native file-path check had been disabled in memory.

That was not the only check. The proof first used the recovered .forceput to set the PostScript-side PermitFileWriting list to [ (*) ]. For %pipe%, parse_file_name() also consulted a cached LockFilePermissions flag. We loaded the font a third time, force-wrote that protected user parameter to false, and used save/restore to synchronize the cached value. The recorded sequence makes the separate gates visible:.

The bounded Debian print job ended with this command proof, writing only a marker in /var/tmp:.

According to recent reports, the scheduler recorded PIPE_RCE_STOPPED=false, and the marker file appeared on the print server. false here means the stopped block completed. The command ran as uid=7(lp), the renderer's account, not as the person who submitted the job.

In a recent development, with the interpreter primitive established, the next question was where a remote user could supply the document. We traced how popular applications invoked image and PDF processing. Three cases show how different the entry points could be.

An attacker only had to send a crafted email to someone using the Roundcube server and have the recipient view the message. The sender needed no Roundcube account. The recipient did not have to click or download the attachment: displaying the email triggered the server-side processing that ran our command.

Recent findings suggest that our attachment was declared as image/jpeg and named quarterly-results.jpg, but its contents were PostScript. Roundcube treated it as an image and automatically requested a thumbnail. The thumbnail path passed the attachment to ImageMagick, which invoked Ghostscript. The document ran our proof command as www-data and produced a thumbnail.

Industry observers note that we reached the same Ghostscript interpreter while WordPress generated a preview for an uploaded PDF. In WordPress Core, media upload privileges were enough: Authors and higher roles have them by default. Plugins using WordPress's upload and preview functions exposed the same path. WordPress's CVE-2026-65640 advisory describes remote code execution on sites using Imagick and Ghostscript. On our Linux systems, that was the stack handling the uploads.

Plugins exposed that processing to visitors without an account. In Forminator, we used a public PDF field configured to store the upload in the Media Library. That caused WordPress to generate attachment metadata and enter the Imagick conversion path. Essential Addons for Elementor's public registration widget provided another route through its upload field. Both chains ran the command as the web-service user. Once the file reached the renderer, the font-loader flaw was the same.

We also reached Ghostscript through CUPS on Debian 13 and other Linux distributions. On Debian 13, we sent an IPP Print-Job to a shared network queue that accepted jobs without authentication. CUPS passed our PostScript document to gstopdf, which started the distribution's Ghostscript with -dSAFER. The command ran on the print server as uid=7(lp).

Our RCE proof executed one fixed command and wrote a marker under /var/tmp. Requiring authentication on the queue blocked the unauthenticated submission. Shared queues that accept network print jobs without credentials expose the renderer to anyone who can reach them.

Industry observers note that the Ghostscript CVE scores the interpreter flaw at 8.5 under CVSS 4.0. That rating uses a local attack vector. Our demonstrations reached the interpreter remotely, through both production services and the applications described here. CUPS supplied a network-exploitable print path; Roundcube supplied an email-based remote exploit; WordPress and its plugins supplied remotely exploitable upload paths. The recorded trials show that these chains were repeatable. The attacker could deliver the exploit remotely, despite the interpreter's local attack-vector classification.

Industry observers note that the first ten rows show Upload2Shell proofs in products or their shipped components. The rows after them trace more upload and preview paths. Each entry gives the access, tested stack or pinned source revision, and the processing step that matters.

Our Ghostscript research also reached Google, Dropbox, and other production services whose names are redacted. The table brings those production services together; the Dropbox and redacted findings have separate roots from the Type 1 bug described in this article.

The renderer's account and the surrounding system controls determine what follows native memory control. That is why the table records process privileges and the observed result alongside the application name.

Here is a complete, self-contained PostScript proof of the native operator write described above. It writes its Type 1 font to Ghostscript's process-local %ram% device, triggers the font-loader flaw, reuses the freed allocation, changes a live mul reference to call sub, and restores the original bytes. No companion font file is needed.

Each step below points to its lines in the full file. The 29 × 11 check returns 319 before and after the write. While the pointer is changed, it returns 18, the result of subtraction. This proof demonstrates native memory control; the command-execution chain described above changes Ghostscript's path-control state instead.

Loading source… Open the complete file.

Sources indicate that the file changes native memory inside the rendering process. It does not execute a shell command or touch host files. On the fixed 10.08.0 build, the dangling-reference lookup failed before the pointer write.

Artifex's first fix checks the operands before .putgstringcopy can fail in copy. That closes the error path we used to recover the privileged store. A subsequent change moves the helper into C and removes its dependence on .forceput.

According to recent reports, the first patch also explains why this kind of operation has been difficult to remove. Artifex was already working to eliminate or minimize its use. As the maintainer put it:.

“it isn't easy to undo 30 years worth of assumptions in the code.” Ken Sharp, Artifex, in the fix for bug 709684.

An internal font loader needed a write that ordinary document code could not perform. An error exposed that authority to the document, and the document used it to violate an object-lifetime rule. The final memory corruption depended on assumptions made at several different layers.

The applications had their own opportunities to interrupt the chain. WordPress released its Core mitigation in 7.0.4 on 12 August, with backports to older supported branches. Its application CVE and the Ghostscript CVE address different points in the processing path. For the CUPS route, queue authentication controls who can submit the document. A policy that prevents a renderer from starting a shell can limit what happens even after the interpreter is compromised.

Industry observers note that the fix has to reach the renderer the application actually uses. Updating the host operating system does not patch a separate copy of Ghostscript inside an existing container image or application bundle. A document worker can therefore keep using vulnerable code after the host's package has been replaced.

It has been revealed that application hardening can close a route into the interpreter as well. The Roundcube sequence illustrates why the order of operations matters: checking a file's real type after generating its thumbnail gives the renderer the first chance to interpret it. For each downstream service, the useful question is what changed in the path from the submitted file to the rendering process.

Artifex released the root fix in Ghostscript 10.08.0 on 8 September 2026. Many distributions have since shipped it, either in that release or as a backport to an older version. Ubuntu published fixes for seven releases; Debian patched Trixie and its development branches.

The coverage is uneven. As of 12 November, Debian still listed Bookworm as vulnerable, Amazon Linux listed a pending fix, and several SUSE branches remained affected or in progress. Applications on those branches can still expose the flaw when their file-processing path reaches the affected Ghostscript package. A distribution name or a recent update to another Ghostscript CVE is not enough to establish that this bug is fixed.

The tables below record the package status for this specific flaw. Older version numbers can include a backported fix; a published fixed version does not establish that every application or container has adopted it.

In a recent development, as of 12 November 2026, the following vendor trackers still listed a vulnerable, affected, or pending Ghostscript package for this exact flaw. These labels describe package status, not a tested remote application path. Check the package actually installed or bundled by each service.

We did not establish whether current RHEL, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, or stable Fedora packages contain the .putgstringcopy fix.

Industry observers note that ubuntu's USN-8949-1, published on 21 October 2026, describes our font-operand finding and lists fixed Ghostscript packages for seven releases. The notice predates the CVE assignment, so it labels this finding “No CVE number.” These are package fixes, not additional remote application tests.

In a recent development, debian's tracker records the first fixed source version for Trixie and unstable. The testing branch later received the upstream-fixed package. Debian 12 remains listed vulnerable in the vendor-status table above.

The records below show packages containing upstream Ghostscript 10.08.0 or an advisory-listed fixed build. A package appearing here does not establish the first fixed date for every architecture or branch.

Industry observers note that fixed Ghostscript builds also reached Windows and macOS packaging channels. The availability of a package does not tell us which Ghostscript binary a particular application uses.

It has been revealed that the dependency problem is easy to miss from the top of an application. Several layers below, a file may enter PostScript or another interpreter that never appeared in the application's security review. A review that checks only whether the upload handler accepts trusted file types can miss a vulnerability in the code that eventually processes them. A penetration test that stops at the same boundary has the same blind spot.

Industry observers note that alongside this Type 1 issue, our broader Ghostscript audit reached production services at Dropbox and other redacted vendors through separate findings. Each program paid its maximum bounty. Their case studies will explain the individual root causes and proofs once we have permission to publish the technical details. The series is organized around the underlying bugs as well as the products.

In a recent development, wordPress released its mitigation on 12 August. Artifex authored the Ghostscript fix on 2 September, committed it on 7 September, and released 10.08.0 on 8 September. We completed the Debian network CUPS proof on 17 September. The Ghostscript CVE was published on 9 November in US Eastern time.

The Debian 13 CUPS chain will be the first full case study and PoC in this series. The other product writeups will follow, with the build, delivery path, exploit result, and vendor response for each. We will add their links to the tables as they appear.

In a recent development, we expect other researchers to find more applications affected by this flaw. The useful place to look is the processing that follows an accepted file: thumbnail generation, metadata extraction, document import, and print conversion. Each can hand an attacker-controlled document to a process with access the sender does not have. Upload2Shell let the document use that access for itself.

Probabilistic data structures in Go, part 2

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antonz

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle.
  • Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).
  • In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, probabilistic data structures give you approximate answers to questions about the data they handle. Does the set contain a certain item? How many unique items are in the collection? What is the 99th percentile in a stream of numbers? How similar are two sets? Unlike deterministic structures, the answers might not be exact, but in return, you can save a lot of memory.

Previously, we reviewed the following data structures: Bloom filter (for checking if an item is in a set), Count-min sketch (for counting items), HyperLogLog (for counting unique items), T-digest (for finding quantiles), and Top-k (for finding the most frequent items).

In this post, we'll talk about other probabilistic structures and compare them to the ones we've already covered. We'll look at how they work and what kinds of guarantees they provide.

All examples use unsure — a package that implements these structures in Go.

Binary fuse filter • UltraLogLog • Log-linear histogram • MinHash.

A binary fuse filter is a set that trades certainty for space, like a Bloom filter1. It can tell you that an item is definitely not in the set, or that it probably is (which might be a false positive). The filter doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

Sources indicate that unlike a Bloom filter, a binary fuse filter is static: you build it once from all the items, and you can't add more later. In exchange, it uses less memory than a Bloom filter with the same false positive rate. For example, a fuse filter for 1,000,000 items with a 0.39% false positive rate takes 1.13 MB (9 bits per item), while a Bloom filter takes 1.51 MB (12 bits per item).

This makes binary fuse filters a good fit for data that is written once and read many times, like the key set of an immutable file in a database (to skip files that don't have the key), or a list of known bad items, such as leaked passwords or malicious URLs.

The fingerprint type (T in New[T]) determines the false positive rate and the memory use:.

According to recent reports, the constructor takes an iterator of items to add to the filter and the expected number of items (0 if unknown). The number is only used to preallocate memory, so a good estimate makes the build faster.

You can check if an item is in the filter, but you cannot add or delete an item, count the number of items, or iterate over them.

The filter2 is an array of b-bit fingerprints (for example, b = 8 for uint8). Each item is hashed to a 64-bit value h, which gives the item's fingerprint f (b bits computed from h) and three positions in the array (cells). The array is filled so that for every item, the XOR of its cells equals f.

To check an item, you compute h, look up its three cells, and compare their XOR with f. For an item in the set, they always match. For any other item, the XOR is a random b-bit value, which matches f with probability 2^-b.

Industry observers note that each check reads three cells, so for large filters it's three cache misses, against one for a blocked Bloom filter. However, since the reads are independent, the CPU can do them concurrently, so the checks are about as fast as with a Bloom filter.

The filter uses the local wyhash3 implementation for hashing. It performs roughly the same as xxh34 but has a much simpler implementation, without SIMD or assembly.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks5, comparing unsure to xorfilter6 (binary fuse by the authors of the paper) and bloom (unsure's own Bloom filter) with 8-bit fingerprints (ns/op, lower is better):.

Memory, bits per item (lower is better):.

It has been revealed that unsure is the same size as xorfilter (same layout) with up to 25% faster checks. Compared to the Bloom filter, it uses up to 36% less memory, with checks as fast or faster, but up to 2.5× slower builds.

Bloom filter overview and how it works. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, binary Fuse Filters paper by Thomas Mueller Graf and Daniel Lemire, 2022. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, reference wyhash implementation by Wang Yi. ↩︎.

Reference xxHash implementation by Yann Collet. ↩︎.

Binary fuse filter benchmarks. ↩︎.

FastFilter/xorfilter by Daniel Lemire. ↩︎.

In a recent development, ultraLogLog is a unique items counter that trades accuracy for space, like HyperLogLog7. It tells you approximately how many distinct items it has seen, no matter how many times each one appeared. UltraLogLog doesn't store the items, so it's much more compact than a regular set.

It has been revealed that ultraLogLog is a newer design (Otmar Ertl, 2024) that uses the space more efficiently: for the same error, it needs about 43% less memory than HyperLogLog. For example, a HyperLogLog sketch with 0.81% standard error takes 16 KB, while an UltraLogLog sketch with 0.86% error takes 8 KB. However, adding, counting, and merging are slower than with HyperLogLog.

UltraLogLog is useful in the same places as HyperLogLog: counting unique visitors, unique search queries, or distinct values in a database column, possibly across many machines or segments.

You can merge sketches to get the total number of unique items from all of them, without counting shared items twice.

The sketch has one setting: the precision p, which gives a relative standard error of 0.782/√(2^p). The default is p=13 with 0.86% error in 8 KB, close to the common HyperLogLog default (0.81% in 16 KB).

Sources indicate that you can add items to a sketch, get the estimated count, and merge sketches. You cannot check if a specific item was added, remove items, or list them.

Sources indicate that hyperLogLog hashes each item and uses the first p bits of the hash to pick one of m = 2^p registers. It calculates the rank (the number of leading zeros in the rest of the hash, plus one) and keeps the highest rank it has seen in the register. Seeing a rank of k suggests there were about 2^k items in the register. The count is estimated from all the registers together.

In a recent development, A HyperLogLog register loses some information: it only keeps track of the highest value, not whether any slightly lower values were seen. These lower values show up at least as often as the highest one, so they can tell a lot about the count.

UltraLogLog8 uses the registers more efficiently. Each register is still one byte, but it stores the highest rank k in the upper 6 bits, and whether k−1 and k−2 were seen in the lower 2 bits:.

It has been revealed that the count estimate uses the FGRA estimator from the UltraLogLog paper. Each register adds a weight based on its value, and the count is calculated as a power of the sum of the weights. Nearly empty and nearly full sketches get special handling, so the estimate stays accurate from zero to billions of items, without bias tables or a separate formula for small counts.

Recent findings suggest that unsure keeps a histogram of register values (256 four-byte counters, 1 KB) updated as the registers change. This way, Count reads the histogram instead of scanning all the registers. Merge checks 8 registers at a time using a few bitwise operations to find which ones the other sketch would change, and only updates those.

The item is hashed once with wyhash, and the 64-bit hash is split into the register index and the rank.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks9, comparing UltraLogLog to unsure's own HyperLogLog and axiom10 (HyperLogLog with LogLog-Beta estimator and sparse mode) (ns/op, lower is better):.

Accuracy and memory, relative RMSE over 1,000 sketches (lower is better):.

It has been revealed that ultraLogLog provides the same accuracy as HyperLogLog with almost half the memory. However, adding, counting, and merging are noticeably slower.

HyperLogLog overview and how it works. ↩︎.

UltraLogLog paper by Otmar Ertl, 2024. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, axiomhq/hyperloglog by Axiom. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, A log-linear histogram is a summary of a stream of numbers that trades accuracy for space. It can give you an approximate median, 99th percentile, or any other quantile of the data. It can also estimate what fraction of the numbers are below a certain value (the CDF). The histogram doesn't store the numbers, so it's much more compact than a sorted list.

In a recent development, for example, to find the exact 99th percentile of 1,000,000 response times, you'd have to keep all of them. With 64-bit floats, that takes 8 MB. A log-linear histogram estimates the same percentile within 0.39% of its true value using about 14 KB — almost 600 times less.

Sources indicate that the error is relative to the value: if the true 99th percentile is 200 ms, the histogram returns a value between 199.2 and 200.8 ms. This guarantee applies to every quantile, from the median to the most extreme outliers. The size of the histogram doesn't depend on the number of values, only on the accuracy you choose and on how wide the range of the values is.

A log-linear histogram is useful when you need percentiles for positive values that cover a wide range, like latencies, file sizes, or prices.

Recent findings suggest that you can merge histograms to gather data from multiple machines or segments (like by hour, endpoint, or region). Merging is exact: a merged histogram is the same as if it had received all the values directly.

Sources indicate that the histogram has two settings: relative error and value range. By default, the error is 0.0039 (0.39%) and the range is from 1e-9 to 1e18. Lowering the error or increasing the range uses more memory.

Industry observers note that you can add numbers to a histogram, estimate quantiles and the CDF, and merge histograms. You cannot remove numbers or list them.

A histogram splits the range of values into buckets and counts how many values are in each one. To estimate a quantile, it adds up the counts starting from the lowest bucket until it reaches the requested rank, then returns a value from that bucket. The accuracy of the estimate depends on how wide the bucket is.

Recent findings suggest that with buckets that have equal widths, like 0–10, 10–20, and so on, every estimate has the same absolute error of ±5 around the bucket's midpoint. So the relative error is very large for small values and unnecessarily small for large values:.

According to recent reports, A logarithmic histogram solves this by making each bucket's width proportional to its value. For example, if the bucket boundaries are powers of 1.02 (1, 1.02, 1.0404, ...), the end of each bucket is 2% larger than its start, so any value in the bucket is within about 1% of the bucket's midpoint. DDSketch11 uses this method. The downside is that finding the right bucket for a value means you have to calculate a logarithm, which is relatively slow.

A log-linear histogram gets almost the same result with cheaper math. First, it splits the values into ranges between powers of two: 1–2, 2–4, 4–8, and so on (these are called octaves). Then it splits every octave into the same number of equal-width buckets. For example, here are three octaves with 4 buckets each:.

It has been revealed that each octave is twice as long as the previous one, so its buckets are twice as wide, and the bucket width grows with the values, as in a logarithmic histogram. Finding the right bucket only takes a few bit operations instead of calculating a logarithm.

HdrHistogram12 is the best-known log-linear histogram. It records integers: the position of the highest 1 bit of a number determines its octave, and the next few bits determine the bucket within the octave.

Unsure works with float64 numbers and finds the bucket in a similar way to HdrHistogram.

IEEE 754 double-precision format.

A float64 in Go (and most other languages) is made up of three parts:.

The number's value is 1.f × 2^e, where 1.f is a binary fraction between 1 and 2.

It has been revealed that the exponent determines the octave, from 2^e to 2^(e+1). The top m bits of the mantissa determine one of the 2^m equal buckets within the octave.

For example, here's the number 5.25 with m=3 (8 buckets per octave). In binary, 5.25 = 1.0101₂ × 2², so the exponent is 2 (stored as 1025), and the mantissa starts with 0101:.

It has been revealed that add finds the bucket for the given number and increases the count. Merge adds the counts bucket by bucket. Quantile adds up the counts from the closer end (the leftmost bucket for q ≤ 0.5, the rightmost bucket otherwise) until it reaches the rank.

The number of mantissa bits m comes from the requested error: the constructor picks the smallest m for which the maximum error doesn't exceed the requested one. The default is m=7: 128 buckets per octave and an error of 0.39%.

A t-digest13 also estimates quantiles, but it limits the error in ranks: Quantile(0.99) returns a value whose rank is close to 99%. A log-linear histogram limits the error in values: Quantile(0.99) returns a value close to the true 99th percentile.

In a recent development, in the middle of the data, the two are pretty similar. But in a long tail, values at nearby ranks can be very different, so even a small error in rank can lead to a massive difference in value. Here is the mean relative error of an 8.5 KB t-digest (δ=100) on 1M values from three distributions: lognormal (as in the benchmarks), Pareto with α=1.5 (a longer tail), and uniform between 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 (no tail):.

A log-linear histogram of about the same size (1% error, 8 KB) has an error below 0.78% for all these cases.

So a log-linear histogram is better for latencies, sizes, and other positive measurements with long tails. A t-digest is better when you need a fixed size no matter what the values are, or when the values can be arbitrarily close to zero.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks14, comparing unsure to hdr15 (log-linear, integers only, fixed range) and dd16 (DDSketch, logarithmic buckets) with a lognormal distribution (ns/op, lower is better):.

Mean relative error at the requested 0.1%, over 1M values (lower is better):.

Memory after adding 1M values (lower is better):.

Industry observers note that unsure adds values as fast as hdr and 5× faster than dd, queries 5–19× faster than hdr and about 35× faster than dd, and merges about as fast as dd and 35–175× faster than hdr. It's slightly less accurate than hdr (using 5× less memory), and more accurate than dd (using 1.4× more memory).

According to recent reports, DDSketch paper by Charles Masson et al., 2019. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that T-digest overview and how it works. ↩︎.

Log-linear histogram benchmarks. ↩︎.

HdrHistogram/hdrhistogram-go by Coda Hale. ↩︎.

Industry observers note that dataDog/sketches-go by Datadog. ↩︎.

MinHash estimates how similar two sets are. It summarizes each set in a short fixed-size signature (for example, 256 numbers). Comparing two signatures gives the approximate Jaccard similarity of the sets: |A∩B| / |A∪B|, the proportion of unique items that both sets share.

The size of a signature doesn't depend on the size of the set, so you can compare two sets of a million items each just by comparing 256 pairs of numbers instead of checking every item. Plus, each set's signature is only calculated once, so comparing lots of sets to each other is relatively cheap.

MinHash is useful for finding near-duplicate documents, like web pages or essays (represented as sets of words or 3-word phrases). It's also useful for finding similar user profiles (as sets of liked items) or overlapping datasets (as sets of keys).

Recent findings suggest that the MinHash sketch has one setting: the signature size k, which gives a standard error of √(J(1−J)/k) for true similarity J. For example, with k=256 and J=0.5:.

In a recent development, you can add items to a sketch, merge sketches, and get and compare signatures. You cannot check if a specific item was added, count the items, remove them, or list them.

Industry observers note that classic MinHash17 hashes every item with k different hash functions. Here are two sets, A = {fox, cat, dog, owl} and B = {fox, dog, emu}, and their item hashes for k=4:.

For each hash function, the set keeps only the smallest hash value among its items. These k minimums are the set's signature. To estimate the similarity of two sets, compare their signatures position by position, count the number of equal values, and divide by k:.

Sources indicate that the estimated similarity (0.5) is different from the actual value (2 shared items / 5 distinct items = 0.4). To get a more accurate estimate, k is usually much larger than in this example.

One permutation hashing18 hashes every item once, with a single hash function, and splits the range of hash values into k equal buckets. Each bucket keeps the smallest hash value among its items. Here are the same sets with k=4, using h1 from above:.

Industry observers note that each bucket works like a separate MinHash over the items in its range. So the bucket minimums form a signature, and comparing two signatures works the same way. But there is a catch: when a set isn't much larger than k, some buckets end up empty (shown as · above), so there's nothing to compare in them.

Recent findings suggest that optimal densification19 solves this by filling each empty bucket with the value from another bucket in the same set. Each empty bucket tries other buckets in a pseudo-random order and copies the value of the first non-empty one:.

Recent findings suggest that this order depends only on the empty bucket's position, so two similar sets tend to fill empty spots with the same values. This makes the estimate work for sets of any size, with about the same error as classic MinHash.

Unsure keeps the k bucket minimums in the sketch. Add and Merge use the original buckets. Densification only happens in Signature, and it makes a copy of the buckets without modifying the sketch.

Industry observers note that each item is hashed once with 64-bit wyhash. Multiplying the hash by k once gives both the bucket and the value to store:.

According to recent reports, densification fills empty buckets in a coordinated way, spreading the copies evenly across the non-empty buckets. This keeps the error close to classic MinHash, and makes densification fast even for small sets.

Here's an excerpt from the full benchmarks20, comparing unsure to dgryski21 (classic MinHash) (ns/op, lower is better):.

RMSE of the similarity estimate at k=256 and J=0.5 (lower is better):.

Unsure adds items 6–70× faster than dgryski, compares signatures at the same speed, has roughly the same accuracy, and uses half the memory.

Classic MinHash paper by Andrei Broder, 1997. ↩︎.

In a recent development, one permutation hashing by Ping Li et al., 2012. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that optimal densification paper by Anshumali Shrivastava, 2017. ↩︎.

dgryski/go-minhash by Damian Gryski. ↩︎.

According to recent reports, bloom filter and HyperLogLog are everyone's favorites, but they're not the only useful probabilistic data structures out there. In some situations, you might find these helpful:.

To use them in Go, try the nalgeon/unsure package:.

  • Recent findings suggest that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold.

Recent findings suggest that the BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1921 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that what's your FI number?
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Industry observers note that the gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that what's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Industry observers note that the gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Sources indicate that here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

Industry observers note that the gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

The annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

It has been revealed that this limit applies per giver, per recipient. That means:.

Recent findings suggest that the IRS adjusts this amount for inflation periodically. Here's how the annual exclusion has changed over the years:.

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

According to recent reports, this is the single most important gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. Gifts received are not taxable income.

When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — right now $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Sources indicate that let's put that in perspective. If you give your daughter $118,000 in one year, you're $100,000 over the annual exclusion. You file Form 709 to report it, and the IRS subtracts that $100,000 from your lifetime exemption. Your remaining exemption drops from $13.61 million to $13.51 million. No tax is owed.

At the 40% top gift tax rate, you'd need to give away more than $13.61 million over your lifetime before any actual tax kicks in. That puts fewer than 0.1% of Americans in gift tax territory.

Sources indicate that key sunset warning: The current $13.61 million exemption is set to be cut roughly in half on January 1, 2026, reverting to approximately $7 million per person (adjusted for inflation) under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act sunset provisions. This has created urgency for high-net-worth families to make large gifts before the window closes.

Filing Form 709 does not mean you owe tax — it simply reports the gift and tracks your lifetime exemption usage.

Industry observers note that one of the most powerful gift tax strategies available is the 529 plan 5-year election. The IRS allows you to front-load up to 5 years of annual exclusion gifts into a 529 education savings plan in a single year.

For 2026, that means you can contribute up to $90,000 (5 x $18,000) to a 529 plan for a single beneficiary in one year. A married couple electing gift splitting can contribute up to $180,000 per beneficiary.

The catch: if you use the 5-year election and then pass away during the 5-year period, a prorated portion of the gift returns to your taxable estate.

Industry observers note that the gift tax and estate tax share the same $13.61 million lifetime exemption. Think of it as one pool of money that covers both gifts during your life and transfers at death.

Every dollar of lifetime exemption you use for gifts during your life reduces the amount available to shelter your estate from tax at death. However, there's a strategic advantage to giving during your lifetime: future appreciation on gifted assets escapes your taxable estate.

In a recent development, example: You give your daughter stock worth $1 million today. You use $982,000 of lifetime exemption ($1M minus $18K annual exclusion). If that stock grows to $3 million by the time you die, the full $3 million — including $2 million in appreciation — is completely outside your estate. That's $2 million that will never be subject to estate tax.

No annual limit, no lifetime exemption usage, no Form 709 required. If your spouse is not a US citizen, a higher annual exclusion applies ($185,000 for 2026) instead of the unlimited deduction.

Gifts are not reported on your income tax return (Form 1040). If you gave more than $18,000 to any single recipient, you file a separate Form 709 (gift tax return) alongside your income tax return. The gift tax affects far fewer people than most assume. With an $18,000 annual exclusion per recipient, a $13.61 million lifetime exemption, and unlimited exclusions for direct tuition and medical payments, the vast majority of Americans can give generously without ever owing a penny in gift tax. The key rules: the giver pays (not the receiver), gifts are not taxable income, and filing Form 709 is just tracking — not a tax bill. For FI families, strategic gifting is one of the most powerful ways to accelerate the next generation's financial independence while reducing your taxable estate.
