Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1261 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • Industry observers note that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

Industry observers note that this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Latest Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

Sources indicate that the table reveals which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

In a recent development, replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In a recent development, in the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

Industry observers note that with @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

The table demonstrates one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Sources indicate that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() highlights which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!

#115251. Breaking: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2233 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2233 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Sources indicate that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

Sources indicate that in an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Sources indicate that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

In a recent development, one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Recent findings suggest that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

Sources indicate that we rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Industry observers note that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

Industry observers note that this effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Think of a shipping tech giant that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

Recent findings suggest that the third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

Industry observers note that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

According to recent reports, adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

Recent findings suggest that they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

It has been revealed that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

According to recent reports, second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

Industry observers note that to find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

According to recent reports, third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

In a recent development, to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

According to recent reports, the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

It has been revealed that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

Sources indicate that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

Sources indicate that to find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that vocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

According to recent reports, vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

According to recent reports, specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

Breaking: TODOs JJ Style

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (237 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Bwc9876

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.
  • Industry observers note that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard.
  • Industry observers note that JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I love using JJ and recently I’ve found a cool way to handle TODOs that works for me.

Industry observers note that usually I’ll put them in a TODO.md file which is pretty standard. But, I forget about this file rapidly and am not very good at remembering to cross stuff off. Also since it’s in-tree I’ll often not want to enhancement it, and then forget to do so later.

Industry observers note that JJ has a cool feature where you can make empty changes, and even write descriptions for them before actually doing work. So what if I just make all the stuff I wanna do later as empty commits?

It has been revealed that pretty nice! When I want to start working on something I’ll rebase it out of my TODO tree and onto some other change.

I need to rebase my “TODO base” forward when i make changes, but because it’s empty it will never have conflicts and can pretty easily move around.

TODOs that depend on other TODOs also naturally fit here, I just make fresh empty commits on top of other empty commits.

I have git.private-commits configured to make sure nothing with the private: prefix will get pushed. This ensures my TODOs stay on my local system. Of course, there are benefits to not doing this.

Anyway that’s about it, not very ground breaking but something I like.

The RMM provider also released a hotfix as a recommended mitigation to address public exploits for the alleged zero-days, which allow for attacker takeover.

N-able is navigating a hectic crisis-management situation after the discovery of more than 30 alleged zero-day flaws in its N-central remote monitoring and management (RMM) platform, as well as the disclosure of exploits allowing attackers to execute commands, create administrator accounts, and escalate privileges to root.

Realizing the critical security nature of the situation, N-able took its hosted N-central environments offline earlier this week across the Americas, Europe, and Asia-Pacific after offensive security researcher Sean Bales on Sunday publicly revealed the flaws, collectively called Able2Shell, and subsequently published a series of exploits for them on the GitHub account "Oracle-Security." N-able also advised customers operating on-premises servers to shut them down until further notice.

"N-able sincerely appreciates the patience, flexibility, and partnership our customers have demonstrated throughout this critical security event," the company wrote in a security revision Wednesday.

Related:Attackers Crash Claude's 'Office Party' Flaw to Run Malicious Code on Linux.

Recent findings suggest that the extraordinary scenario has major repercussions for the entire endpoint management industry, including managed service providers (MSPs) and IT managers who broadly use N-central to monitor, manage, and secure customer devices and networks remotely. The risk for people of vulnerable platforms is significant because of the "extraordinary privileges" these RMM platforms have "because they need them to do their jobs," observes Gene Moody, field chief technology officer (CTO) for autonomous endpoint management provider Action 1.

Industry observers note that N-able and other RMM platforms can engage in critical tasks such as script execution, software deployment, and remote administration, often across many thousands of endpoints, Moody notes. The downside? "That also makes them incredibly attractive targets," he says.

Sources indicate that indeed, with public exploit code available, attackers are already scanning for vulnerable systems, although no exploitation has yet been observed, N-able reported in a security patch Wednesday. The company moved fast to remedy some of the most critical flaws, releasing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (build 2026.4.1.26) on Tuesday to address seven CVEs associated with them; the company indicates it also plans to release further security updates.

Flaws covered by the N-able hotfix are tracked as the following: CVE-2026-125883, which covers multiple XXE vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125878, which covers multiple OGNL Injection vulnerabilities; CVE-2026-125879, a local privilege escalation flaw; CVE-2026-125880, described as stored XSS via MMS3 patch metadata; and CVE-2026-125881, a schema validation flaw.

Related:Google, Partners Disrupt 1.3 Million-Device-Strong XCPE Botnet.

The patch also addresses CVE-2026-125882, which enables remote code execution (RCE) via file repository upload path traversal and was discovered by Nate Fair of Sprocket Security; and CVE-2026-91000, which leads to local privilege escalation via insecure IPC Channels.

Though Bales disclosed 33 separate flaws, some of them are steps in longer exploit chains built from other entries on the same list, according to a report from Tenable's Research Special Operations published today. All in all, Bales listed four exploit chains, with the XXE chain emerging as potentially the most significant of the complications, according to Tenable.

"The researcher describes the XXE chain as credential-free, and N-able's record for CVE-2026-125883 lists no privileges and no user interaction as required," the Tenable team wrote. That chain exploits an unauthenticated XXE flaw in N-central's service-import functionality and can ultimately turn an unauthenticated network request into a complete compromise of a central IT management system.

Indeed, the CyberSec Guru called the credential-free XXE exploit the "centerpiece of the release" and went into detail about how it can be exploited to create an attacker entry point into a system in a blog post updated Tuesday.

Related:'Aokigahara' Stealer Targets 'Developer Keyrings' & AI Assistants.

It has been revealed that moreover, once an attacker has compromised a platform, the other vulnerabilities can help expand their access to take over privileged internal sessions and ultimately execute commands on the underlying server, paving the way for cross-customer compromise, according to the post. This scenario is especially concerning for MSPs managing infrastructure on behalf of many organizations.

The recently disclosed flaws are not N-central's first time dealing with a significant security incident. In August 2025, CISA added two N-central vulnerabilities, CVE-2025-8875 and CVE-2025-8876, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after they were exploited in the wild.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, in August 2026, attackers exploited an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18556), subsequently finding a way around N-able's initial fix through a related vulnerability, CVE-2026-18577. The second incident allowed attackers to gain administrative access to vulnerable N-central servers and use the platform's Take Control feature to access managed systems.

The recurrence of vulnerabilities in the same management platform raises broader questions about the security of RMM infrastructure, particularly given the extensive access these tools provide to MSPs and their customers, Moody indicates.

"I see this as yet another warning in a recent wave of attacks on these platforms; how much authority endpoint management platforms concentrate," he notes. "They are essential, but MFA and role-based access cannot contain every platform compromise.".

All in all, the situation has created a significant security quagmire for N-able and its customers, who — given that exploitation of the flaws could be imminent — are advised to apply the hotfix where necessary as well as take other immediate mitigation steps.

"The clock is ticking for anyone not taking this seriously," Moody observes, advising that any affected organization "keep on-premises N-central offline until N-able provides safe restoration instructions," while preserving logs before making any changes.

Moreover, they should "review authentication and administration since at least the beginning of November, just because this is exposed does not mean it was not leveraged prior to disclosure," he warns.

In a recent development, researchers from Huntress also advised organizations affected to review login and authentication activity from Nov. 8 onward for unexpected or unauthorized access, according to a blog post published Monday. If they find it, they should involve incident response, as it could indicate that an attacker conducted RCE or privilege escalation on the server.

Huntress also advised organizations to examine audit logs for secondary indicators of compromise — such as anomalous remote access sessions or fresh scripts being deployed — since as during previous N-central exploitations, "threat actors were observed 'spraying' downstream environments with unauthorized scripts and tools.".

Noting that CISA's March guidance called for least privilege, phishing-resistant MFA and second-administrator approval, Moody notes he would go even further this time to protect N-able environments by keeping critical secrets and signing keys outside the platform, and making endpoints independently verify cryptographically signed approval for high-impact operations.

According to recent reports, "Stealing a credential, or even controlling the console, should not automatically confer that authority," he states. "A login should no longer be considered enough to authorize protected operations.".

Her areas of expertise include enterprise technology, cybersecurity, business, and culture. During her long career, Elizabeth has lived and worked as a full-time journalist in Phoenix, San Francisco, and New York City. She specializes in news coverage and analysis, using her years of experience to look at the current state of cybersecurity with a critical gaze. #115247. NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2108 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Feyor ↗ Open Full Page

NixOS bring-up on an Alibaba RISC-V board

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2108 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Feyor

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.
  • It’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU.
  • I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the process of scouring Alibaba for a cheap Versal devkit, I unexpectedly came into possession of a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V SoC.1.

It’s a cool board: there’s a ridiculous amount of IO exposed by the baseboard, not to mention 8 cores clocked at 1.9 GHz is nothing to sniff at for a RISC-V CPU. I’m not sure I could recommend buying any RISC-V SoC currently2, but all these distros that are starting to support RISC-V need to run tests somewhere that isn’t Spike/QEMU.

I decided to make this board into a NixOS build server so I could learn more about the state of RISC-V support in NixOS and to get some practice in Linux bringup.

My complete A210 NixOS configuration can be found here; I confirmed sound, HDMI, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi, ethernet, and the GPU were all working, but YMMV.

Nix makes cross compiling to RISC-V a breeze:.

In a recent development, it really is that easy—building pkgs.hello will produce a bona fide RISC-V executable (you don’t even need a Nix file for one-off builds, just run nix build nixpkgs#pkgsCross.riscv64.hello). Some black magic in callPackage ensures that compile-time tools are built for buildPlatform and build artifacts are built for hostPlatform.

In the process of compiling over a thousand packages I only ran into two issues: a problem with rust-bindgen using the wrong version of clang and ministream not being properly configured for cross compilation, neither of which was specific to RISC-V.

It has been revealed that that having been remarked, I did run into some pretty bizarre OOM issues for some of the heavy hitters like Clang and GFortran. I was seeing >9GB memory usage per linking process(!) when compiling from x86_64-linux, which will rapidly exhaust all of your memory if you have max-jobs/cores set to sane values. I sidestepped this concern by temporarily nerfing build parallelism into oblivion and running the offending builds overnight:.

Sources indicate that I don’t (yet) have access to a RISC-V remote Nix builder, but even if I did, it’s substantially faster to cross compile everything from my desktop. Cross compilation can get a little wonky with Nix flakes because you have to encode the buildPlatform in the output schema somehow, but nixosConfigurations does not allow nesting (nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux-a210 is valid, but nixosConfigurations.x86_64-linux.a210 isn’t).

My solution to this is to expose the relevant build artifacts of the NixOS configuration (ISO + flashing script) under packages.${system} by creating a “wrapper” NixOS configuration for each buildPlatform that extends nixosConfigurations.a210:.

This way nixosConfigurations is agnostic to buildPlatform, and cross compilation is straightforward—running nix build .#image on an x86_64-linux machine will use x86_64-linux as the buildPlatform, as one would expect.

Ok, so the goal is to boot U-Boot FSBL -> OpenSBI -> U-Boot SSBL -> Linux -> NixOS userspace, using the vendor’s Buildroot scripts as reference.

Recent findings suggest that using vendor forks of U-Boot/Linux/OpenSBI is a simple matter of overriding src and sprinkling in a few patches (almost always to fix compiler warnings that have been promoted to errors in the latest version of GCC/Clang in nixpkgs). All we really have to do is slot in the vendor kernel by setting boot.kernelPackages = pkgs.linuxPackagesFor pkgs.linuxA210;.

It has been revealed that armed with a bootloader and NixOS image, I plugged in the A210 to my MacBook and turned on Fastboot flashing mode, but to my dismay macOS refused to enumerate the device. Initially I figured the board was a lemon (due to it being a freebie and all), but I wasn’t ready to give up hope that easily.

I pored over the datasheet looking for alternative boot methods, and I investigated using PD resistors to force QSPI boot (using NORbert in lieu of a real QSPI device) to bootstrap into Linux userspace, at which point I could flash the eMMC directly without relying on Fastboot. But before pulling out my soldering iron I decided to try plugging the board into a different computer, which instantly detected the board. D’oh!

Industry observers note that ok, so Fastboot works3 and I’m able to load the flasher firmware and program eMMC (I based my Fastboot payload on openEuler’s A210 guide instead of the vendor’s script which flashes 7(!) different partitions), but after that I still got dead silence on UART. At this point I was pretty suspicious of my serial connection, so I decided to test it on a Pi Pico: lo and behold, it turns out leaving my BMP’s vRef pin floating was the culprit.

After losing several hours and my dignity to the aforementioned skill concern, I was greeted with the following panic:.

Judging from the above register dump, something seems to be amiss with OpenSBI itself:.

This confirmed my suspicion that the illegal instruction was from an ISA extension (in this case, a vector instruction). Initially I didn’t understand why this occurred: why would a CPU trap on an instruction it supports? I consulted the ISA spec and discovered that executing a vector instruction without the vector context bits of the mstatus register configured properly will result in the exact illegal instruction exception that I was seeing.

Sources indicate that so roughly what was happening was the processor was context switching to OpenSBI where the vector context was not enabled, but certain operations like memset were optimized to use vector extensions because OpenSBI was compiled with -march=rv64gv. I conjecture that the vendor didn’t run into this issue because they compiled OpenSBI with a GCC toolchain that didn’t support vector instructions, but who’s to say? Backporting a patch that sets -march=generic did the trick, and now we’re making it into U-Boot stage 2.

At this point I could boot Linux from eMMC manually, but I wanted to take the time to do things “right”. I prefer the more generic distro boot to the hard coded boot command the vendor came up with, so I decided to roll my own board header.

Ok—now we’re able to get most of the way through the initrd before UART abruptly goes silent. Fortunately, the last message makes the problem pretty clear:.

According to recent reports, it’s a bit of a hack, but I decided to set clk_ignore_unused on the kernel command line just to see if we could get more logs. Imagine my surprise when after reflashing, the board makes it all the way into NixOS userspace with no concerns! Although I steeled my resolve to go spelunking in the device tree to find which clock was not marked as critical, I decided not to waste my time when I realized the vendor also sets clk_ignore_unused in their kernel cmdline. ¯\_(ツ)_/¯.

Recent findings suggest that I would be remiss if I didn’t mention that running an old kernel in the current era of AI-assisted kernel vulnerability disclosures hitting LKML every other week does not exactly help me sleep better at night. I looked into backporting patches for Dirty Frag and co., but if the attacker has access to my tailnet I’m already cooked.

So now that I can SSH in, we’re done, right? Well, the vendor explicitly advertises support for Vulkan/OpenGL ES, so I decided I couldn’t call this finished until I brought up the GPU.

This requires support in both the kernel (a driver to talk to the actual GPU hardware) and in userspace (implementing a uniform interface like Vulkan over the device-specific API). For the former, The vendor opts to ship a kernel module with no source; a firmware blob (with a device tree to make sense of it) I can generally understand, but I don’t get shipping kernel modules, and here’s why:.

According to recent reports, kernel modules rely on the pertinent ABIs of the kernel being built against and the kernel the module will run on being nearly identical. If CONFIG_MODVERSIONS is set in your Kconfig (which it should be), the kernel will refuse to load a module if its vermagic (basically an ABI checksum) doesn’t match that of the running kernel. I’m using the vendor’s fork of Linux, so the vermagic matches exactly—so far so good.

Recent findings suggest that but comparing vermagics only checks for identical function prototypes; there are several Kconfig options that can change the size, alignment and layout of kernel data structures like struct module. Many of these are security or debugging related, and I’ve done enough kernel exploitation in my day to understand that there are good reasons to introduce this seemingly unnecessary binary incompatibility.

The upshot is I can’t use the vendor kernel module unless I massage NixOS’s Kconfig into producing a kernel that passes Linux’s ABI compatibility smell checks.

While searching for an alternative solution, I was pleasantly surprised to learn that my GPU is already supported in upstream Linux and Mesa! In my naïvety I thought “great, we’ll clone Linux 6.18, run make -M=$PWD/drivers/gpu/drm/imagination -C vendor-linux/lib/modules/6.6.0/build modules and we’ll have a perfectly compatible driver!”.

Industry observers note that however, several changes in the DRM subsystem thwarted my attempt for a clean port, and in a fit of desperation (SLOP WARNING) I vibe ported the driver from the 6.18 kernel tree to an external module I could compile against the vendor fork of Linux 6.6. Adding a ton of code I did not write or understand is especially not good for software running with supervisor-level permissions; using this code feels like taping a “pwn me” sign to my back.

If you’re following along, I want to emphasize that my slop driver is only for using the A210’s GPU, and if you chose to use it you should first sic your own clanker on the source to make sure I’m not punking you.4 Alas, this is (in my opinion) still better than trying to use the prebuilt kernel module.

I was getting a bit fed up with the “compile-nix copy-kernel hang” loop, so I took a few minutes to setup a MCP server for Ghidra. I then tasked Codex (without Daybreak) with comparing the vendor-supplied kernel module with the slop that was ported from newer Linux.

Industry observers note that the issue was identified and fixed within 3 minutes, whereas printk debugging and debugfs abuse got nowhere in several hours. Static analysis for the win!

After ironing out the kinks in the kernel side, we need to coax Mesa into letting us use it by setting PVR_I_WANT_A_BROKEN_VULKAN_DRIVER, after which we can successfully draw triangles!

OpenGL-rendered spinning cube textured with a particular book cover.

HDMI capture of glmark2-es2-wayland running under Zink (context for texture).

macOS USB support kinda sucks (I’ve encountered similar challenges with the Altera USB-Blaster III); if a device isn’t detected, try a different computer.

(In an attempt to upgrade my USB drivers I made the generational fumble of updating to macOS 27, which makes Asahi Linux look stable in comparison.).

Never assume something works just because you think it should (trust, but verify).

The multitude of kernel configuration options makes kernel module API/ABI compatibility a pain; having source makes the problem tenable but still nontrivial.

Industry observers note that overall, this was a fun (if not unexpected) project. I have fond memories of designing a OoO RISC-V CPU with all the bells and whistles during my time at uni, so this nerd snipe was particularly gratifying for me.

It’s a bit of a shame that this machine won’t see a lot of use, but I anticipate that will change as RISC-V adoption continues to grow. Also, I am still flabbergasted that NixOS is completely slept on by SoC suppliers; I eagerly await the day NixOS will eat Yocto/PetaLinux/Buildroot’s lunch.

I paid a frankly too-good-to-be-true price of $1.2k for an Alinx VD100, and so I was disappointed but not surprised when I instead received some random $300 RISC-V curio. Thankfully I was able to get a full refund and keep the board; I think the “scam” here is to write off the cost of excess inventory as misshipments instead of surplus. ↩︎.

It has been revealed that I’m loathe to recommend a Microchip product, but the PolarFire SoC Discovery costs $130 and doubles as both a RV64GC SoC and an FPGA. ↩︎.

I couldn’t get the board to enter Fastboot mode after I flashed a bootloader, but this was fine because I could run fastboot usb 0 in U-Boot instead. ↩︎.

Sources indicate that this is not to say you shouldn’t audit the other stuff too, but if you were pwned by something other than the PowerVR driver, at least you could take solace in the fact that a human (me) had the last laugh. ↩︎.

To call this GPU “dinky” would be an understatement; for comparison, my RX 6700 XT scores 26230 on the same benchmark. ↩︎.

#115246. Latest Update: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3177 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done.
  • Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Noted It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

Sources indicate that we built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Sources indicate that figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Recent findings suggest that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Industry observers note that then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Recent findings suggest that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

According to recent reports, we call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

It has been revealed that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

In a recent development, table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Sources indicate that training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

Sources indicate that what does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

Recent findings suggest that in a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

In a recent development, thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly upcoming solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

According to recent reports, and bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

According to recent reports, if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 demonstrates which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

Industry observers note that after training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

According to recent reports, average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

Recent findings suggest that the observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

It has been revealed that overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

In a recent development, pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

It has been revealed that figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

It has been revealed that the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

Industry observers note that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

According to recent reports, these results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

According to recent reports, selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Recent findings suggest that training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each enhancement generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

It has been revealed that zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

It has been revealed that that explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

Recent findings suggest that no ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

It has been revealed that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

Industry observers note that A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

In a recent development, we used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

In a recent development, so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

Recent findings suggest that figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

In a recent development, we partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

It has been revealed that figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

It has been revealed that figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

Industry observers note that when an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Enhancement the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:.

Industry observers note that start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Grafana 13.3 Adds Shared Dashboard Variables and Notebooks.

Nov 21, 2026 2 min read.

Grafana Labs has released Grafana 13.3 with cross-dashboard variables that let teams manage shared dashboard controls in one place. The release also introduces Notebooks for collecting panels and investigation notes in a document that colleagues can share.

Sources indicate that the release announcement describes cross-dashboard variables as a public preview across all Grafana editions. Teams can define a variable once and use it in multiple dashboards, avoiding separate configurations for a selector such as an environment or a region. Grafana indicates managing those copies separately can lead to configuration drift.

According to recent reports, cross-dashboard variables address a longstanding user request. In a 2021 GitHub discussion, Grafana user Darth-Bobo described having to maintain the same variables separately across dashboards, warning that configuration differences could become "unmanageable over time". More recently, an early tester described shared variables as useful for evaluating Git Sync without Terraform templating.

It has been revealed that variables can have global scope, which makes them available throughout a Grafana organisation, or folder scope, which limits them to dashboards in the same folder. An editor can add the available variables from a dashboard sidebar, either individually or all at once. Viewers can still change the selected value on a dashboard, while the variable configuration remains centrally managed.

Teams running Grafana themselves must enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle to try the preview. Grafana places the management screen under Dashboards > Variables, separate from the dashboard editor where people add the shared controls.

Sources indicate that notebooks are also in public preview across all editions. A notebook can hold panels from dashboards or Explore alongside written observations, with findings from Grafana Assistant included as well. Teams can use the document to record how they investigated an issue or to prepare a post-incident review with relevant panels already in place.

It has been revealed that owners can create a notebook manually or through Grafana Assistant, then save and share it. Grafana is rolling the feature out gradually to Grafana Cloud. Self-managed installations need the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle enabled.

Industry observers note that grafana’s Notebooks joins similar investigation-document workflows from other observability vendors. Datadog Notebooks combines live graphs with rich text and supports simultaneous editing, inline comments and reusable postmortem templates. New Relic Notebooks, generally available since August 2026, combines NRQL queries, visualisations and Markdown, with natural-language query translation and notebook-wide variables.

Sources indicate that the release also changes how Grafana Assistant builds dashboards. In public preview, dashboard plans let a user describe what they want to monitor and review a proposed layout in chat before building it. The blueprint covers the title and the proposed panels, including visualisation types and variables. A read-only preview lets the user refine the plan before choosing to build and save the dashboard.

According to recent reports, A separate Assistant feature, Undo turn, is generally available across all editions. It restores the previous dashboard state after an Assistant edit, including when one request changed multiple panels. The Assistant dashboarding guide notes that undo is unavailable if the dashboard has changed since the Assistant's edit.

Grafana 13.3 also previews a visual refresh with revised themes and interface components. Grafana Labs says the visual refresh preserves existing navigation and workflows and introduces no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins using standard Grafana components and theme tokens pick up the new appearance; those with custom styling can migrate separately. Self-managed owners can enable grafana.visualDesignRefresh to try it and switch back to the previous design.

Breaking: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package).
  • The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub.
  • In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

In a recent development, the Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We initiative to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

It has been revealed that select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script releases its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Industry observers note that each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

In a recent development, each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (909 w)

Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Darkreading ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Darkreading

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.
  • A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.
  • Industry observers note that that's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.

A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.

Industry observers note that that's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens. Then, they're using these tokens to access and steal information.

Joseph Keyes, author of the blog post and cyber threat intelligence analyst at ReliaQuest, wrote that this latest wave of targets are "likely" those that didn't pay Luna Moth's first extortion demand, with this second hit coming weeks-to-months later.

Sources indicate that A ReliaQuest spokesperson tells Dark Reading that these firms were targeted a second time because the group knows these organizations can be socially engineered (so it tries again with different tactics), for a second set of data. Moreover, as fewer organizations are paying, law firms make a good fit to target, because "their client data is highly sensitive and the reputational hit from exposure is severe, so repeated leverage is worth the effort.".

Related:3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack.

In the initial variants of the attack, Luna Moth would reach out as IT support and trick victims into connecting to Windows' built-in remote assistance tool. It would then download data directly. This time, the group sent blank-subject emails from a free email address with a broken PDF masquerading as a business report; the "report" would then fail to open. The attacker would use this pretext to reach out soon after, posing as IT support responding to a malicious alert, while at the same time offering to fix the PDF.

Once on a video call, the "IT support" directs the target to turn on screen-share functionality so they can direct the target through a "fix." The attacker then tells the target to open Microsoft Copilot from the Web browser on their work laptop, open the browser's developer tools, find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph, and copy the application's access token.

The attacker instructs the target to paste the token into a public text-sharing site the attacker can access. Finally, the attacker gives the token to its own folder and downloads files through the Microsoft Graph API.

This social engineering tactic requires no malware and no vulnerability. It relies solely on tricking a target into giving an access token, effectively a master key into the front door of an organization. The use of IT support to "fix" a technical issue evokes ClickFix, as both techniques rely on human problem-solving tendencies to trick an end user.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery.

Recent findings suggest that the ReliaQuest spokesperson states the firm considers this attack representative of a gap in how controls are scoped within an organization. Because the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and handed over "willingly," security red flags do not go off.

"A token is a bearer credential, so it works from anywhere until it expires, unless CAE [Continuous Access Evaluation] with strict location enforcement (or token binding) applies," the spokesperson claims. "Similar to device code phishing, the user completes a legitimate flow, so MFA is satisfied. The weakness is the assumption that authentication equals ongoing trust. Microsoft's defaults, such as the 60- to 90-minute lifetime and CAE not being enforced by default, make it easier.".

It has been revealed that reliaQuest recommends that organizations turn CAE on by default, block browser developer tools and token-inspection pages on managed browsers, and restrict remote-support and screen-sharing tools where there's no business need. Additionally, it may be wise to inform employees of the ways threat actors attempt to steal credentials from employees.

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform.

As the blog post put it, "Tell users that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback.".
